1.pericope_label: The Lord shewed me, and, behold, two baskets of figs were set before the temple of the Lord: one basket had very good figs, and the other basket had very naughty figs, which could not be eaten

schools.summary: Fixes the date after the first deportation and early in Zedekiah's reign, reads the seeing as an inward event, explains the removal of the craftsmen as policy and display, and takes the two sorts of fig from the horticulture of the country.

Insists the vision is exhibited rather than encountered, and reads the temple setting as a court of judgment in which both halves of the nation stand arraigned and neither lot came from the enemy's will.
Attends to the ordering of the text and to the natural history behind the emblem, identifying the uneatable fruit with the crude winter fig.
Draws the pastoral moral, that the first and heaviest sufferers are not therefore the worst sinners.

debates.question: What does it signify that the baskets were set before the temple?

positions.view: they are a votive offering, first-fruits or tithes brought to the Lord, which the remiss priests had not come out to receive
not an offering at all and nothing to do with first-fruits; the baskets figure the people themselves appearing before their God at the altar of burnt-offering
the temple is God's tribunal, so that the whole nation stands at the bar and the division of its lot proceeds from him

debates.question: Do the good and bad figs describe the character of the two groups or only their sentences?

positions.view: punishment only: the captive king suffers for his own sins and is not good in himself, but was chastened more gently than those left behind
a real difference of worth, the exiles including genuinely good men and better in any case than a Jerusalem growing worse

debates.question: What were the figs that could not be eaten?

positions.view: the winter crop, caught in its crude state before the spring
fruit left behind on the tree, bruised and decayed

outliers.reading: Alone proposes reordering the opening verse, putting the notice of the captivity first and the showing of the baskets last, on the ground that this book transposes not only whole chapters but parts of verses.
Will commit no further than that the showing was probably a vision, where the others argue the point.

themes: The Lord shewed me, and, behold, two baskets of figs were set before the temple of the Lord, after that Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon had carried away captive Jeconiah the son of Jehoiakim king of Judah, and the princes of Judah, with the carpenters and smiths, from Jerusalem, and had brought them to Babylon.
One basket had very good figs, even like the figs that are first ripe: and the other basket had very naughty figs, which could not be eaten, they were so bad.
Then said the Lord unto me, What seest thou, Jeremiah? And I said, Figs; the good figs, very good; and the evil, very evil, that cannot be eaten, they are so evil.

4.pericope_label: Like these good figs, so will I acknowledge them that are carried away captive of Judah: I will set mine eyes upon them for good, and I will give them an heart to know me

schools.summary: Works from the grammar outward: the phrase for their good governs the looking rather than the sending, the clause about returning is causal and not conditional, and the promised building is a spiritual regeneration whose effects can be traced in the record of the exile.

Reads the promise as wholly gratuitous, making repentance the effect of pardon rather than its cause, and takes the heart given as understanding, so that conversion is God's work from beginning to end.
Grounds the favour partly in the exiles themselves, who had not led in sin, had been carried away by the example of others, and were now penitent and accepting the punishment of their iniquities.

debates.question: On what ground do the captives receive this favour?

positions.view: they had not sinned so deeply, were led rather than leaders in sin, and are now penitent and submissive under the rod
on no ground in them: the clause reads for they shall return, not when, and the turning itself is the gift, so repentance is the fruit of mercy and not its condition

debates.question: What is promised in the building and the planting?

positions.view: not merely the restoration of their former civil well-being but a spiritual regeneration of the people
God's watchful providence over them and their return, whose effects appear in their actual condition in Babylon and after it

outliers.reading: Sets out three constructions of the doubled promise to build and not pull down: that the negative is emphatic, so far from plucking up that he will plant; that it is sequential, having pulled down he will now build; or that it promises permanence, planting so as never to pluck up again. He prefers the first.

Reads the heart given as the understanding rather than the affections, and guards the phrase with the whole heart against perfectionism, since no one puts off every fleshly affection at once; what it excludes is dissimulation, not imperfection.

themes: Again the word of the Lord came unto me, saying,

Thus saith the Lord, the God of Israel; Like these good figs, so will I acknowledge them that are carried away captive of Judah, whom I have sent out of this place into the land of the Chaldeans for their good.
For I will set mine eyes upon them for good, and I will bring them again to this land: and I will build them, and not pull them down; and I will plant them, and not pluck them up.
And I will give them an heart to know me, that I am the Lord: and they shall be my people, and I will be their God: for they shall return unto me with their whole heart.

8.pericope_label: And as the evil figs, which cannot be eaten, so will I give Zedekiah the king of Judah, and his princes, and the residue of Jerusalem, to be a reproach and a proverb

schools.summary: Traces the wording to the covenant curses of the Law and follows the Egyptian remnant forward into the later history of the book and beyond it.

Keeps the comparison one of sentences rather than characters, presses the Hebrew for its exact force, and turns the promise of the land against those who thought an inheritance held by covenant could not be forfeited.
Reads the threat through its outcome in the war and after it, and closes on the fate of those who never returned.

debates.question: How far does this sentence reach?

positions.view: the seventy years began it, but its complete fulfilment came in the destruction of the nation by the Romans, to which the words more particularly point
it fell in the Chaldean war and the years following, when many died by sword and famine and many more never returned at all

outliers.reading: Fastens on the preposition, observing that the text says consumed from off the land rather than in it, since they were not destroyed at home but removed and left to pine away by degrees elsewhere, the sword standing for the war that carried them out.
Alone follows the Egyptian company beyond the prophecy, making them the nucleus of the Jewish population of Egypt which in time set up a rival temple at Leontopolis.

themes: And as the evil figs, which cannot be eaten, they are so evil; surely thus saith the Lord, So will I give Zedekiah the king of Judah, and his princes, and the residue of Jerusalem, that remain in this land, and them that dwell in the land of Egypt:
And I will deliver them to be removed into all the kingdoms of the earth for their hurt, to be a reproach and a proverb, a taunt and a curse, in all places whither I shall drive them.
And I will send the sword, the famine, and the pestilence, among them, till they be consumed from off the land that I gave unto them and to their fathers.
